summary:
What did I build?
I built the Fire Activity Atlas, a web app unifying NASA FIRMS fire thermal detections from MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m). It aggregates annual CSVs by country, 0.5° cell, and day, displaying them via a map, rankings, a daily calendar, and charts. Users can filter by country or custom map area and export data. Built with Node.js, vanilla JS, HTML, and CSS (zero backend dependencies), it was tested with 2025 Mexico data (64,966 MODIS; 272,810 VIIRS detections).
How does it address the challenge?
Because FIRMS data is fragmented and VIIRS detects smaller fires than MODIS, the datasets aren't directly comparable. My solution has three parts:
Integration: Converts VIIRS counts to MODIS units using monthly factors from overlapping days.
Anomaly detection: Compares each day to the same dates (±7 days) across other years to flag critical streaks via adjustable thresholds.
Visual exploration: Uses maps, calendars, and charts to reveal trends without coding.
Built for historical analysis (loading CSVs at startup), its limits are clear: figures show thermal detections (not burned area), totals mirror MODIS, data is unfiltered by source/confidence, the method lacks external validation, and anomalies require multi-year data.
Why is it important?
Analyzing wildfire trends requires long, comparable datasets. Using only Node.js and public CSVs, this tool removes technical barriers, letting anyone explore historical patterns and compare regions for planning without coding.
details:
. What does it do exactly? 

The project is a web application that explores historical fire thermal detection data from NASA FIRMS. It takes annual CSV files by country from two sensors, MODIS and VIIRS, aggregates them, and displays them in a single interface. With it, you can: 

  • Check a ranking of countries by number of detections; 
  • Visualize the areas with the highest activity on a map, grouped into 0.5° grid cells; 
  • Review a daily calendar (year × day of the year) showing the intensity or anomaly of each day; 
  • Analyze monthly series and annual totals; 
  • Identify critical periods, defined as streaks of days with unusually high activity; 
  • Filter by country or by a rectangular area drawn on the map; 
  • Export the harmonized daily series in CSV format. 

Scope. The application does not work in real time. It only reads the CSV files available in the data/ folder, and it does so only once when the server starts. It does not query the FIRMS API while running, nor does it update automatically. Detections represent satellite thermal observations, not burned area or the number of individual fires. 

2. How does it work? 

a) Data ingestion. The ingest.js module reads each CSV via streaming, line by line, allowing it to process large files. The sensor, year, and country are extracted from the file name, which must follow the format sensor_YYYY_Country.csv (for example, modis_2025_Mexico.csv). From each row, only the latitude, longitude, and acquisition date are used. Each row counts as one detection and is stored in memory using the structure country → 0.5° cell → day → [MODIS count, VIIRS count]. 

b) MODIS–VIIRS harmonization. MODIS is used as the baseline because it has the longest record. VIIRS detects smaller fires, so its count is converted to "MODIS units" using a factor calculated for each month of the year: the sum of MODIS detections divided by the sum of VIIRS detections across days where both sensors have data. When a month has 30 or fewer VIIRS detections, the overall ratio is used. For each day, if both sensors are present, their values are averaged (MODIS and the converted VIIRS); if only one is present, that single value is used. 

c) Anomalies and critical periods. Each day is compared, using a z-score, against the same days of the year (±7 days) across the other loaded years. A critical period is a streak of consecutive days whose anomaly exceeds a configurable threshold (by default, 2σ for at least 3 days). Periods are ranked by their maximum anomaly. This calculation requires multiple years of data; with only a single year, there is no baseline for comparison and the anomaly defaults to zero. 

d) Server and API. The server is built with Node.js's built-in http module, with no external dependencies. It exposes five routes: /api/health, /api/meta, /api/ranking, /api/cells, and /api/daily, in addition to serving the frontend files. 

e) Interface. The browser requests data from the API, repeats the harmonization for the selected country or area, and renders the map (Leaflet), charts (Chart.js), and calendar (canvas). If there are no CSV files in data/, the system generates synthetic demo data—clearly labeled in the interface—that does not correspond to real observations. 

Data used in testing. A total of 844 FIRMS files containing 49,429,387 detections were loaded. 

3. Benefits 

  • Integrates two sensors with different resolutions and operating periods into a single comparable record. 
  • Makes it easy to identify seasonality, outlier years, and periods of unusual activity through visualizations. 
  • Allows analysis by country or by a user-defined custom area. 
  • Uses data from an official, public source (NASA FIRMS), uploaded directly by the user. 
  • Lightweight installation: requires only Node.js 18 or higher, with no additional packages needed. 
  • Documents its methodology and limitations directly within the interface and allows results to be exported. 

4. Objective and expected results 

The objective is to provide a tool to explore historical fire activity patterns, detect unusual conditions, and pinpoint critical periods by country or area. The expected result is a comparable long-term overview, provided multiple years of data are loaded. With a single year—such as in the test run with Mexico 2025—the tool displays counts, the map, and the intensity calendar, but cannot calculate anomalies or critical periods. 

Limitations affecting the results 

  • Figures represent thermal detections, not burned area. 
  • When both sensors are present, the harmonized total is practically equal to that of MODIS, because VIIRS is scaled to that baseline. VIIRS provides the daily curve shape and extends the series, but does not alter that total. 
  • Data is not filtered by source type or confidence level. In the test files, 16.4% of MODIS detections and 14.5% of VIIRS detections correspond to non-vegetation sources (type other than 0). 
  • The three VIIRS satellites (SNPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21) are treated as a single sensor. 
  • Area selection has a 0.5° resolution. 
  • The harmonization method was not validated against an external reference. 
  • Cloud cover and satellite overpass times affect detection counts. 

5. Programming languages and tools 

  • JavaScript: Used on the backend with Node.js (server.js, ingest.js, demo.js), in the browser (app.js), and in the shared logic between both (harmonize.js). 
  • HTML and CSS: Interface structure and styling (index.html, styles.css). 
  • Python 3 (standard library only): Optional script for downloading data from the FIRMS API (fetch_firms.py). 
  • Browser libraries (loaded via CDN): Leaflet 1.9.4 (map), Chart.js 4.4.1 (charts), and topojson-client 3.1.0 (boundaries). 
  • External data and services: Base imagery from NASA GIBS (Blue Marble) with Esri World Imagery as a fallback, country boundaries from Natural Earth (world-atlas), and fonts from Google Fonts. 
  • Testing: node:test, with 3 unit tests covering harmonization and critical periods. 
  • Containers: Dockerfile based on node:20-alpine. 
  • Data formats: CSV (input), JSON (API), and TopoJSON (boundaries). 

6. Hardware and software 

Software required to run: Node.js 18 or higher (or Docker) and a modern web browser with an internet connection, which is needed to load the libraries, boundaries, fonts, and map tiles. Python 3 is only required if using the optional download script. 

Hardware required to run: No specialized equipment is needed; it runs on a standard computer or server. All aggregated data is kept in memory, so RAM usage increases with the number of loaded CSV files. In the test run with 337,776 detections, the server started up smoothly. 

How is the project creative?

  • Seasonal harmonization. Instead of applying a single conversion factor from VIIRS to MODIS, a separate factor is calculated for each month of the year, since the relationship between the two sensors shifts with the seasons. When a month has very little data, the global ratio is used.
  • Year × day calendar. Displays all years against the days of the year in a single view, in either intensity or anomaly mode. This makes atypical seasons recognizable at a glance—patterns that would otherwise be hidden in a standard line chart.
  • Adjustable critical periods. The user defines how many standard deviations and how many consecutive days count as unusual activity, and the list recalculates instantly.
  • Open-ended exploration. Users can analyze a specific country or draw a rectangle directly on the map, with no coding required.
  • Technical simplicity. It runs on Node.js with zero external packages to install, making it easy to execute and audit.

What factors did we take into account?

  • Data honesty. The interface explicitly states that the figures represent thermal detections rather than burned area, and clearly explains the methodology and its limitations.
  • Comparability. Because the two sensors have different spatial resolutions and operating periods, putting them on a single unified scale was essential.
  • Data volume. Files are read via streaming and aggregated into 0.5° grid cells to handle hundreds of thousands of rows without overwhelming memory.
  • Open and verifiable source. It uses only public NASA FIRMS data, uploaded directly by the user.
  • Robustness. The map includes a fallback tile service in case the primary one fails, and the server validates all API parameters.
  • Ease of use. It features result exporting, a Spanish-language interface, and minimal installation requirements.
